title: The wing that wasn't deforming
intro: A structural monitoring rig reports a large displacement-gradient tensor on a wing section during a turn, and the dashboard flags it as strain approaching limits. The strain gauges disagree. Open the clues.

facts.label: The alert
facts.value: The monitoring system computes the displacement-gradient tensor from optical markers and reports a magnitude well above the strain threshold. It fires every time the aircraft banks.

facts.label: The gauges
facts.value: Bonded strain gauges on the same section read near zero throughout the manoeuvre. Two independent gauge sets agree with each other.

facts.label: The tensor
facts.value: Symmetric part P = ½(A + Aᵀ) is essentially zero. Skew part Q = ½(A - Aᵀ) carries almost the entire magnitude, with a clean zero diagonal.

facts.label: The manoeuvre
facts.value: The alert magnitude tracks bank rate, not aerodynamic load. In steady level flight at high load factor, the alert is silent.

facts.label: The markers
facts.value: Optical marker tracking calibrated this month; residuals within tolerance. The markers are tracked in the ground frame, not the body frame.

facts.label: The threshold
facts.value: The strain limit was taken from the material spec and has not changed since the rig was commissioned.

question: What actually failed?
choices: The strain gauges have debonded and are under-reporting
The dashboard measures the raw gradient tensor, whose skew part is rigid-body rotation, not deformation — decomposing A = P + Q shows the strain half is near zero and nothing is being damaged
The material strain limit was transcribed wrongly and is too low
Optical marker calibration has drifted during high-g manoeuvres
debrief: The decomposition answers this in one line: `A = ½(A + Aᵀ) + ½(A - Aᵀ)`, and the split is **unique**. The symmetric half P is deformation — stretch, compression, shear, the thing that fatigues metal. The skew half Q is rigid-body rotation, which moves every marker and damages nothing. Here P ≈ 0 and Q carries the magnitude, so the wing turned; it did not stretch. The marker clue explains why: tracking in the **ground frame** means a banking aircraft produces a large gradient purely from the frame rotating underneath it. Two details make this a clean diagnosis rather than a guess. Q's diagonal is exactly zero, which is forced by skew-symmetry (aᵢᵢ = -aᵢᵢ) and is the signature of rotation rather than a small strain. And the alert tracks **bank rate rather than load factor** — strain follows aerodynamic load, so a signal that ignores load and follows rotation was never strain. Two independent gauge sets agreeing is the corroboration; suspecting them was always the weaker hypothesis. Fix the dashboard to report P, and the alert becomes meaningful instead of merely loud.
